fixes.explanation: Wicked kings is a fair guess, baker. But Peter doesn't name any kings. He says “…there will be false teachers among you.” (2 Peter 2:1) Teachers are the word he picked.
That's right. Peter says they “…will secretly introduce destructive heresies…” (2 Peter 2:1). Secretly means quietly, not out in the open where everyone can see. So this one is False, friend.

Yes, baker. Peter says “Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed.” (2 Peter 2:2) Defamed means its name gets dragged around unfairly. Truth is the way that takes the hit.

That's it. Peter says “In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words.” (2 Peter 2:3) Greed is when someone eyes the whole cookie box and wants your share too. And the tool they use is words that deceive.

The king of Egypt doesn't show up in Peter's verse. He says God reduced the cities to ashes “…as an example of what is coming on the ungodly…” (2 Peter 2:6). That's the purpose he gives. Peter never says who was meant to see it.

Peter actually says it outright. Lot, the righteous man God rescued, lived among them day after day and “…was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard…” (2 Peter 2:8). I think that's a heavy way to live. He was righteous and he saw and heard those deeds.

That's the whole point of the ifs. Peter says “…the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment.” (2 Peter 2:9) Noah and Lot were the rescued ones. The angels were placed in chains of darkness to be held for judgment (2 Peter 2:4). The ancient world and the cities were brought to destruction.

That's right. Peter says “Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings.” (2 Peter 2:10) Timid doesn't fit that description. Bold and unafraid is the picture, baker, and it's not a compliment here.

Peter doesn't put the angels on the false teachers' side at all. He says that “…not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges…” (2 Peter 2:11). The angels hold back before the Lord. The false teachers, Peter says, are unafraid to slander glorious beings (2 Peter 2:10).
Peter says they blaspheme “…in matters they do not understand…” (2 Peter 2:12). Studying for years isn't what he describes. What he says is that they do not understand.

Peter doesn't say where they learned anything. In the verse before, he says the angels don't dare bring such slanderous charges (2 Peter 2:11). The false teachers blaspheme “…in matters they do not understand…” (2 Peter 2:12). Angels aren't the source he names.

Peter says it the other way around. He says “They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight.” (2 Peter 2:13) Broad daylight means in the day, not after dark. So the carousing isn't waiting for the sun to go down.
That's right, friend. Peter says “They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight.” (2 Peter 2:13) Broad daylight, not after dark. A pleasure, he says, and in the middle of the day.

Yes, baker. Peter says they are “…blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you.” (2 Peter 2:13) They're at the feast alongside the believers. Peter names that as the very moment they revel in their deception.

Prayer would be a nice setting, but it isn't the one Peter gives. He says they are “…reveling in their deception as they feast with you.” (2 Peter 2:13) The word is feast, so picture a meal, not a prayer meeting. Peter never says they do it while praying.

Wise is a nice guess, baker, but Peter says “they seduce the unstable.” (2 Peter 2:14) Unstable means not steady, like a stamp pressed down on a wobbly counter. Those shaky ones are who he names, not the wise.
Peter does talk about greed, so wealth makes sense as a guess. But he says “they seduce the unstable.” (2 Peter 2:14) Unstable is who he names. Wealth isn't what he points to there.

Yes, friend. Peter says the false teachers have wandered off to follow “…the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness.” (2 Peter 2:15) Balaam is the prophet from the story in Numbers 22. The thing Balaam loved was the wages of wickedness.

That's a quiet, lovely thing to love, but Peter names something else. He says they follow “…the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness.” (2 Peter 2:15) Balaam is the one who loved those wages. The wilderness doesn't come up.

Lions have their own Bible moments, like Daniel in the lions' den (Daniel 6:16). But Peter says Balaam “…was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey…” (2 Peter 2:16). A donkey was the one who did the rebuking. No lion in this one, baker.

That's it. Peter says they “…entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error.” (2 Peter 2:18) Those are people just getting away from others who live in error. Peter says the false teachers use lofty but empty words to entice them. Big-sounding and hollow, that's the bait.

Peter's target is different. He says they “…entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error.” (2 Peter 2:18) Those are people just getting away from others who live in error. That's the group he names.

That's right. Peter says “They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity.” (2 Peter 2:19) Then he explains: “For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.” So the ones handing out freedom are slaves themselves.

That's what Peter says. If they have escaped the corruption of the world and are then entangled and overcome by it again, “…their final condition is worse than it was at first.” (2 Peter 2:20) I think that's a sad turn.

I'd like that to be true, but Peter says the opposite. For those who are entangled and overcome again, he writes “…their final condition is worse than it was at first.” (2 Peter 2:20) Worse, not better.

That's the picture. A dog returns to its vomit, and a sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud (2 Peter 2:22). Both of them go back. That's what Peter says of those who return to what they escaped.

That's the opposite of Peter's picture. The sow in his proverb is washed, but then she “…goes back to her wallowing in the mud.” (2 Peter 2:22) The dog returns to its vomit too. The picture is going back, not staying clean.
